claim: Brn3a is expressed in the vast majority of DRG and trigeminal ganglion neurons beginning at approximately E11.
source: Brn3a, a POU-domain transcription factor, is expressed in the vast majority of DRG and trigeminal ganglion neurons beginning at ∼E11 (Fedtsova and Turner, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fedtsova and Turner, 1995.

claim: The Brn3aCKOAP allele has one loxP site in the 5′ untranslated region, a second loxP site 3′ of the 3′ UTR, and an alkaline phosphatase reporter distal to the second loxP site.
source: Neurons expressing Brn3a can be visualized using a Brn3a conditional knockout allele (Brn3aCKOAP) that has one loxP site in the 5′ untranslated region (UTR), a second loxP site 3′ of the 3′ UTR, and an alkaline phosphatase (AP) reporter distal to the second loxP site (Badea et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Badea et al., 2009.

claim: Cre-mediated excision of the Brn3a coding region and 3′ UTR activates expression of AP by placing it under the control of the Brn3a promoter.
source: Cre-mediated excision of the Brn3a coding region and 3′ UTR activates expression of AP by placing it under the control of the Brn3a promoter.
evidence: The claim is based on the described mechanism of the genetic construct.

claim: Sparse Cre-mediated recombination was obtained using a Neurofilament Light Chain (NFL)-IRES-CreER knock-in allele and low dose Tamoxifen.
source: In the present study, sparse Cre-mediated recombination was obtained using a Neurofilament Light Chain (NFL)-IRES-CreER knock-in allele and low dose Tamoxifen (Rotolo et al., 2008; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rotolo et al., 2008 and reference to Materials and methods.

claim: NFL-IRES-CreER is widely expressed in projection neurons and not expressed in non-neural tissue.
source: NFL-IRES-CreER was chosen as the source of Cre-recombinase because it is widely expressed in projection neurons, it is not expressed in non-neural tissue, and it produces a relatively low level of CreER.
evidence: The claim is stated as a rationale for choosing this genetic tool.

claim: The combination of Brn3aCKOAP with ROSA26-CreER activates AP expression in muscle and connective tissue as well as in DRG neurons.
source: By contrast, the combination of Brn3aCKOAP with a ubiquitously expressed CreER (ROSA26-CreER; Badea et al., 2003) activates AP expression in muscle and connective tissue as well as in DRG neurons, thereby compromising the clarity with which cutaneous sensory afferents can be imaged.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Badea et al., 2003.

claim: Brn3a+/− and Brn3a+/+ mice are indistinguishable in appearance and overall health.
source: Brn3a+/− and Brn3a+/+ mice appear to be indistinguishable in appearance and overall health and individual Brn3a+/− DRG neuronal cell bodies do not differ in appearance or number relative to Brn3a+/+ controls (Xiang et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Xiang et al., 1996.

claim: Individual Brn3a+/− DRG neuronal cell bodies do not differ in appearance or number relative to Brn3a+/+ controls.
source: Brn3a+/− and Brn3a+/+ mice appear to be indistinguishable in appearance and overall health and individual Brn3a+/− DRG neuronal cell bodies do not differ in appearance or number relative to Brn3a+/+ controls (Xiang et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Xiang et al., 1996.

claim: In Brn3a+/− DRG neurons, a Brn3a-dependent negative feedback regulatory system leads to nearly wild type levels of Brn3a transcripts and other Brn3a-regulated transcripts.
source: Importantly, Trieu et al. (2003) and Eng et al. (2004) have shown that, in Brn3a+/− DRG neurons, a Brn3a-dependent negative feedback regulatory system leads to nearly wild type levels of Brn3a transcripts and other Brn3a-regulated transcripts.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Trieu et al. (2003) and Eng et al. (2004).

claim: It is unlikely that Brn3a+/− DRG neurons differ functionally or morphologically from their wild type counterparts.
source: Thus, it seems unlikely that Brn3a+/− DRG neurons differ functionally or morphologically from their wild type counterparts.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the previous evidence about Brn3a expression levels.

claim: The survey of afferent arbor morphologies was conducted with back skin because this territory includes a wide variety of cutaneous sensory types and its large area facilitates the identification of well-isolated AP-stained arbors.
source: The present survey of afferent arbor morphologies was conducted with back skin because this territory includes a wide variety of cutaneous sensory types and its large area facilitates the identification of well-isolated AP-stained arbors.
evidence: The claim is stated as a rationale for the experimental design.

claim: In mature pigmented mice, melanin in skin and hair confounds full-thickness skin imaging.
source: In mature pigmented mice, melanin in skin and hair confounds full-thickness skin imaging.
evidence: The claim is stated as a technical challenge.

claim: Skin pigmentation is temporarily lost at P21, the midpoint of the approximately 2-day telogen phase of the highly synchronous first hair cycle.
source: This difficulty was circumvented by harvesting the skin at P21, the midpoint of the ∼2-day telogen phase of the highly synchronous first hair cycle (Müller-Röver et al., 2001; Alonso and Fuchs, 2006). During this time window, skin pigmentation is temporarily lost (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Müller-Röver et al., 2001 and Alonso and Fuchs, 2006, and by Figure 1A.

claim: For the Brn3aCKOAP/+; NFL-IRES-CreER/+ genotype, 200 μg, 500 μg and 1 mg of intraperitoneal Tamoxifen produced approximately 5, approximately 50 and >500 labeled and well isolated arbors per back skin at P21.
source: Titration of the Tamoxifen dose at gestational day (GD)17 showed that for the Brn3aCKOAP/+; NFL-IRES-CreER/+ genotype, 200 μg, 500 μg and 1 mg of intraperitoneal (IP) Tamoxifen produced ∼5, ∼50 and >500 labeled and well isolated arbors per back skin at P21 (Figure 1B,C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B, C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: At the highest Tamoxifen dose (1 mg), individual sensory arbors cannot be resolved.
source: At the highest Tamoxifen dose (1 mg), individual sensory arbors cannot be resolved (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A total of 101 P21 Brn3aCKOAP/+; NFL-IRES-CreER/+ back skins were analyzed following maternal exposure to 100, 200, 250, or 500 μg of Tamoxifen at GD17.
source: A total of 101 P21 Brn3aCKOAP/+; NFL-IRES-CreER/+ back skins were analyzed following maternal exposure to 100, 200, 250, or 500 μg of Tamoxifen at GD17.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental dataset.

claim: The average surface area per back skin was 15.53 cm2.
source: With an average surface area of 15.53 cm2 per skin, this corresponds to a total of 1569 cm2 examined for AP stained sensory arbors.
evidence: The claim is based on measurements from the experimental dataset.

claim: A total of 1569 cm2 of back skin was examined for AP stained sensory arbors.
source: With an average surface area of 15.53 cm2 per skin, this corresponds to a total of 1569 cm2 examined for AP stained sensory arbors.
evidence: The claim is based on calculations from the experimental dataset.

claim: The fraction of back skin surface area occupied by well-separated AP+ sensory arbors varied from approximately 0.2% to approximately 15%.
source: The fraction of back skin surface area occupied by well-separated AP+ sensory arbors varied from ∼0.2% to ∼15%.
evidence: The claim is based on measurements from the experimental dataset.

claim: A total of 719 arbors that appeared by visual inspection to be free from overlap were characterized further.
source: A total of 719 arbors that appeared by visual inspection to be free from overlap were characterized further (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental dataset and is supported by Figure 1C,D.

claim: 77 full arbors for nine different arbor types were traced using Neuromantic.
source: To analyze arbor morphologies in detail, we traced 77 full arbors for nine different arbor types (Figure 1D) using Neuromantic, a publicly available reconstruction program.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods and is supported by Figure 1D.

claim: The set of labeled sensory neurons corresponds to the intersection of the expression domains of the Brn3a and NFL genes.
source: The set of labeled sensory neurons is predicted to correspond to the intersection of the expression domains of the Brn3a and NFL genes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the genetic labeling strategy.

claim: Brn3aCKOAP is expressed in nearly all DRG neurons.
source: Although Brn3aCKOAP is expressed in nearly all DRG neurons (Badea et al., 2012), expression of the NFL-IRES-CreER knock-in allele presumably mirrors the abundance of the neurofilament light chain and is therefore enriched in sensory neurons with large axon diameters.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Badea et al., 2012.

claim: Expression of the NFL-IRES-CreER knock-in allele is enriched in sensory neurons with large axon diameters.
source: Although Brn3aCKOAP is expressed in nearly all DRG neurons (Badea et al., 2012), expression of the NFL-IRES-CreER knock-in allele presumably mirrors the abundance of the neurofilament light chain and is therefore enriched in sensory neurons with large axon diameters.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the known properties of neurofilament light chain.

claim: The current survey likely covers only a fraction of the morphologic diversity of cutaneous sensory arbors.
source: Thus the current survey likely covers only a fraction of the morphologic diversity of cutaneous sensory arbors.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the limitations of the labeling method.

claim: The abundances of different arbor types within this set is not related in any simple way to the actual abundances of these types within the skin.
source: We also note that the abundances of different arbor types within this set is not related in any simple way to the actual abundances of these types within the skin because (1) variations in the level of NFL-IRES-CreER expression in different neuronal types will bias their representation, (2) larger arbors tend to be under-represented because the probability of arbor overlap increases with size, and (3) the representation of the most abundant arbor classes was limited by the investigators to a number sufficient for statistically robust analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple sources of bias in the sampling method.

claim: Variations in the level of NFL-IRES-CreER expression in different neuronal types will bias their representation.
source: We also note that the abundances of different arbor types within this set is not related in any simple way to the actual abundances of these types within the skin because (1) variations in the level of NFL-IRES-CreER expression in different neuronal types will bias their representation, (2) larger arbors tend to be under-represented because the probability of arbor overlap increases with size, and (3) the representation of the most abundant arbor classes was limited by the investigators to a number sufficient for statistically robust analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the properties of the genetic labeling system.

claim: Larger arbors tend to be under-represented because the probability of arbor overlap increases with size.
source: We also note that the abundances of different arbor types within this set is not related in any simple way to the actual abundances of these types within the skin because (1) variations in the level of NFL-IRES-CreER expression in different neuronal types will bias their representation, (2) larger arbors tend to be under-represented because the probability of arbor overlap increases with size, and (3) the representation of the most abundant arbor classes was limited by the investigators to a number sufficient for statistically robust analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the selection criteria for isolated arbors.

claim: 10 morphologically distinct cutaneous arbor types were identified.
source: In the paragraphs that follow we describe the identification and characterization of 10 morphologically distinct cutaneous arbor types.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The 10 arbor types were initially distinguished by visual inspection.
source: These types were initially distinguished by visual inspection.
evidence: The claim describes the method of classification.

claim: Statistical analyses of morphologic properties confirmed the divisions of the 10 arbor types.
source: Subsequent statistical analyses of their morphologic properties (arbor area, axon length, number of axon branches, type of sensory ending specialization, number of hair follicles contacted, and lamination depth within the skin) have confirmed those divisions.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The smallest afferent arbors target single Merkel cell clusters (touch domes) or single hair follicles.
source: The smallest afferent arbors appear to target single Merkel cell clusters (touch domes) or single hair follicles.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experimental data.

claim: Most of the follicles targeted by I-FACE and I-FALE arbors appear to be guard (tylotrich) hairs based on their large diameter (approximately 50 μm).
source: In the latter category (I-FACE and I-FALE), most of the follicles appear to be guard (tylotrich) hairs based on their large diameter (∼50 μm).
evidence: The claim is based on morphological measurements from the experimental data.

claim: All cutaneous sensory axons enter the dermis from subdermal nerves and are invariably broken during the skin dissection, generally within several hundred microns of their terminal arbors.
source: The assumption that MCA, I-FACE, and I-FALE afferents target single Merkel clusters or single follicles must be qualified by noting that all cutaneous sensory axons enter the dermis from subdermal nerves and are, therefore, invariably broken during the skin dissection, generally within several hundred microns of their terminal arbors.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the anatomy and the dissection procedure.

claim: An individual axon can innervate more than one Merkel cell cluster based on neurobiotin filling experiments in neonatal mice.
source: This caution is given extra weight by evidence that an individual axon can innervate more than one Merkel cell cluster based on neurobiotin filling experiments in neonatal mice. In these experiments several slowly adapting type I (SAI) low threshold mechanoreceptor axons were observed to innervate two adjacent Merkel cell clusters (Woodbury and Koerber, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Woodbury and Koerber, 2007.

claim: In P21 skin preparations, 20/20 labeled MCA arbors targeted only isolated Merkel cell clusters, with no other labeled MCA arbors seen within a radius of >350 μm.
source: However, in our P21 skin preparations 20/20 labeled MCA arbors targeted only isolated Merkel cell clusters, with no other labeled MCA arbors seen within a radius of >350 μm.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experimental data.

claim: I-FALE arbors have lanceolate endings that encompass almost the entire circumference or approximately half of the circumference of an individual guard hair follicle.
source: The top row of images in Figure 2A shows two arbors with lanceolate endings that encompass almost the entire circumference [I-FALE (A13-11)] or approximately half of the circumference [I-FALE (A13-12)] of an individual guard hair follicle.
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2A.

claim: MCA arbors innervate all or nearly all Merkel cells within a single semi-circular Merkel cell cluster.
source: Two examples of arbors that innervate all or nearly all Merkel cells within a single semi-circular Merkel cell cluster are seen in the bottom row of images in Figure 2A.
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2A.

claim: MCA terminal arbors encompass the posterior 50–75% of the circumference of the central follicle.
source: Like Merkel cell clusters, the MCA terminal arbors encompass the posterior 50–75% of the circumference of the central follicle.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experimental data.

claim: BE arbors have dense and finely branched processes that encompass an area of 0.5–1 mm in diameter and ramify at a depth of 5–10 μm from the skin surface.
source: A distinct class of arbors, which we refer to as bushy ending (BE), have dense and finely branched processes that encompass an area of 0.5–1 mm in diameter and ramify at a depth of 5–10 μm from the skin surface (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 3.

claim: The terminal branches of BE arbors ramify within a narrow stratum.
source: As with all arbor types described here, the terminal branches of the BE arbors ramify within a narrow stratum (Figure 3B; top image).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 3B.

claim: BE arbors have total axon lengths of approximately 10 cm with approximately 1,000 branch points.
source: BE arbors have total axon lengths of ∼10 cm with ∼1,000 branch points (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 3F.

claim: TE arbors have only 20–80 branch points and exhibit relatively sparse coverage of an irregular area of 300–500 μm in diameter at a depth of approximately 20 μm from the skin surface.
source: Another distinctive type of arbor, which we refer to as thick ending (TE), has only 20–80 branch points and exhibits relatively sparse coverage of an irregular area of 300–500 μm in diameter at a depth of ∼20 μm from the skin surface (Figure 4G–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 4G–J.

claim: A distinctive feature of the TE class is a thickening of the terminal 50–100 μm of its branches.
source: As its name implies, a distinctive feature of the TE class is a thickening of the terminal 50–100 μm of its branches, a feature that is presumably related to its sensory function (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 4G.

claim: LD-FALE arbors have a sparsely branched arbor that innervates between 2 and 36 follicles.
source: One type, low-density follicle-associated lanceolate endings (LD-FALE), has a sparsely branched arbor that innervates between 2 and 36 follicles (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 4A–D.

claim: LD-FALE arbors encompass territories of 1–2 mm in diameter, with total axon lengths of only 5–35 mm and with only 5–40 branch points.
source: These arbors encompass territories of 1–2 mm in diameter, but with total axon lengths of only 5–35 mm and with only 5–40 branch points (Figure 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 4I.

claim: In nearly every instance, the opening of the 'C' of lanceolate endings faces the anterior of the mouse.
source: In nearly every instance, the opening of the 'C' faces the anterior of the mouse (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 8E.

claim: HD-FALE is the most commonly encountered arbor type, accounting for approximately 50% of all AP+ arbors.
source: The most commonly encountered arbor type, high density follicle-associated lanceolate ending (HD-FALE), accounts for ∼50% of all AP+ arbors (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 1D.

claim: The lanceolate endings of HD-FALE arbors localize approximately 50 μm beneath the skin surface.
source: The lanceolate endings of HD-FALE arbors localize ∼50 μm beneath the skin surface, and each arbor contacts ∼90% of the follicles within an area that ranges from ∼200 μm to ∼1 mm in diameter (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 5.

claim: Each HD-FALE arbor contacts approximately 90% of the follicles within an area that ranges from approximately 200 μm to approximately 1 mm in diameter.
source: The lanceolate endings of HD-FALE arbors localize ∼50 μm beneath the skin surface, and each arbor contacts ∼90% of the follicles within an area that ranges from ∼200 μm to ∼1 mm in diameter (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 5.

claim: Most HD-FALE arbors have areas less than 10^6 μm^2 (mean ± SD of 3.4 ± 3.2 × 10^5 μm^2) and innervate fewer than 50 follicles (mean ± SD of 30 ± 22).
source: Although most HD-FALE arbors have areas less than 106 μm2 (mean ± SD of 3.4 ± 3.2 × 105 μm2) and innervate fewer than 50 follicles (mean ± SD of 30 ± 22), this type varies substantially, with arbor areas ranging from 105 μm2 to 2.5 × 106 μm2 and the number of follicles innervated ranging from 6 to 153 (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 5D.

claim: HD-FALE arbor areas range from 10^5 μm^2 to 2.5 × 10^6 μm^2 and the number of follicles innervated ranges from 6 to 153.
source: Although most HD-FALE arbors have areas less than 106 μm2 (mean ± SD of 3.4 ± 3.2 × 105 μm2) and innervate fewer than 50 follicles (mean ± SD of 30 ± 22), this type varies substantially, with arbor areas ranging from 105 μm2 to 2.5 × 106 μm2 and the number of follicles innervated ranging from 6 to 153 (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 5D.

claim: For the 12 traced HD-FALE arbors, the mean axon length (excluding the lanceolate endings) was approximately 2 × 10^4 μm and the mean number of branch points was approximately 75.
source: For the 12 traced arbors, the mean axon length (excluding the lanceolate endings) was ∼2 × 104 μm and the mean number of branch points was ∼75.
evidence: The claim is based on measurements from the experimental data.

claim: Individual HD-FALE endings wrap around their target follicles to variable extents, covering the full circumference or as little as approximately 30% of the circumference.
source: As seen with I-FALE and LD-FALE arbors, individual HD-FALE endings wrap around their target follicles to variable extents (Figure 5A–C), covering the full circumference or as little as ∼30% of the circumference.
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 5A–C.

claim: SA-FACE arbors were rarely observed (8 out of 719 arbors).
source: One type, which we refer to as small area follicle-associated circumferential ending (SA-FACE) was rarely observed (8 out of 719 arbors).
evidence: The claim is based on counts from the experimental data.

claim: SA-FACE arbors contact few follicles (mean ± SD of 3.8 ± 1.1), generally have fewer than 20 branch points, and have diameters of approximately 200 to approximately 500 μm.
source: SA-FACE follicles contact few follicles (mean ± SD of 3.8 ± 1.1), generally have fewer than 20 branch points, and have diameters of ∼200 to ∼500 μm (Figure 4E,F,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 4E,F,I.

claim: LA-FACE arbors contact many follicles (mean ± SD of 197 ± 73), including occasional guard hair follicles, within territories of 1–2 mm in diameter.
source: By contrast, arbors designated as large area follicle-associated circumferential endings (LA-FACE) contact many follicles (mean ± SD of 197 ± 73), including occasional guard hair follicles, within territories of 1–2 mm in diameter (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 6.

claim: LA-FACE arbors have axon lengths (excluding the circular endings) that cluster in the 8–15 cm range, with approximately 200 branch points per arbor.
source: These arbors have axon lengths (excluding the circular endings) that cluster in the 8–15 cm range, with ∼200 branch points per arbor.
evidence: The claim is based on measurements from the experimental data.

claim: The fraction of follicles innervated within the LA-FACE arbor territory ranges from 19% to 79% with a mean of 57%.
source: The fraction of follicles innervated within the arbor territory ranges from 19% to 79% with a mean of 57%.
evidence: The claim is based on measurements from the experimental data.

claim: There is a clear trend for larger LA-FACE arbors to exhibit a lower mean density of innervated follicles.
source: There is a clear trend for larger arbors to exhibit a lower mean density of innervated follicles (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 6E.

claim: LA-FE arbors have axons arranged in two narrowly stratified tiers: an inner arbor at a depth of approximately 70 μm and an outer arbor at a depth of approximately 10 μm from the skin surface connected by >50 vertical branches.
source: In this class, the axons are arranged in two narrowly stratified tiers: an inner arbor at a depth of ∼70 μm and an outer arbor at a depth of ∼10 μm from the skin surface are connected by >50 vertical branches (Figures 7A,B and 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 7A,B and 8D.

claim: The inner arbor of LA-FE exhibits sparse but relatively uniform coverage of an area approximately 3 mm in diameter with a total axon length of approximately 10–15 cm.
source: The inner arbor exhibits sparse but relatively uniform coverage of an area ∼3 mm in diameter with a total axon length of ∼10–15 cm.
evidence: The claim is based on measurements from the experimental data.

claim: The outer arbor of LA-FE exhibits denser and relatively uniform coverage of an area approximately 4 mm in diameter with a total axon length of 50–100 cm.
source: The outer arbor exhibits denser and relatively uniform coverage of an area ∼4 mm in diameter with a total axon length of 50–100 cm (Figure 7B–D, Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 7B–D, Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The torso of a P21 mouse is only approximately 4 cm in length.
source: By way of comparison, we note that the torso of a P21 mouse is only ∼4 cm in length.
evidence: The claim is based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: The axons of LA-FE arbors appear to lack terminal specializations.
source: The axons appear to lack terminal specializations.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experimental data.

claim: The relatively uniform coverage within the outer arbor of LA-FE is not achieved by a strict self-avoidance mechanism, as there are numerous examples of axon crossings within the same arbor.
source: The relatively uniform coverage within the outer arbor is not achieved by a strict self-avoidance mechanism, as there are numerous examples of axon crossings within the same arbor.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experimental data.

claim: Within the inner arbor of LA-FE, axon crossings are rare.
source: However, within the inner arbor, axon crossings are rare.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experimental data.

claim: Clear qualitative distinctions between most arbor types are apparent based on the presence or absence of follicle-associated endings, the type of specialized structure elaborated by the sensory endings, and whether or not the arbor targeted single guard hair follicles or Merkel clusters.
source: In the descriptions above, clear qualitative distinctions between most arbor types are apparent based on the presence or absence of follicle-associated endings, the type of specialized structure elaborated by the sensory endings, and whether or not the arbor targeted single guard hair follicles or Merkel clusters.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The quantitative analysis of continuous variables reinforces the distinctions between arbor types and provides a clear separation between LD-FALE vs HD-FALE and SA-FACE vs LA-FACE.
source: The quantitative analysis of continuous variables in Figure 8 reinforces those distinctions and, in addition, provides a clear separation between the two pairs of arbor types that are most closely related by qualitative criteria, LD-FALE vs HD-FALE and SA-FACE vs LA-FACE.
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 8.

claim: BE, LA-FACE, and LA-FE arbor types show the tightest clustering of arbor area values.
source: This analysis reveals different degrees of clustering of area values within different arbor types, with BE, LA-FACE, and LA-FE types showing the tightest clustering.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of Figure 8A.

claim: Variation in arbor areas within HD-FALE, LD-FALE, and TE types spans two orders of magnitude.
source: By contrast, variation in arbor areas within HD-FALE, LD-FALE, and TE types spans two orders of magnitude.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of Figure 8A.

claim: The areas of SA-FACE and LA-FACE arbors are non-overlapping.
source: Figure 8A also shows that the areas of SA-FACE and LA-FACE arbors are non-overlapping.
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 8A.

claim: BE arbors show the highest axon length:area ratio and LD-FALE arbors show the lowest ratio.
source: Extending this analysis to the correlation of axon length and arbor area illustrates striking differences in arbor density, with the high density BE arbors showing the highest length:area ratio and the sparse LD-FALE arbors showing the lowest ratio (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 8B.

claim: There is a clear separation between LA-FACE and LA-FE arbor types in a plot of axon length vs arbor area.
source: This plot also shows a clear separation between LA-FACE and LA-FE arbor types and between these and other types.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of Figure 8B.

claim: LA-FACE arbors innervate >100 follicles per arbor and SA-FACE arbors innervate <10 follicles per arbor.
source: In this figure we introduce a new parameter, the 'innervation index', defined as the number of follicles innervated per μm2 of skin. It is apparent that the two classes of arbors with circular endings, LA-FACE and SA-FACE, differ markedly in number of follicles innervated: >100 per LA-FACE arbor and <10 per SA-FACE arbor (Figure 8C, left panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 8C.

claim: SA-FACE arbors have a lower mean innervation index than LA-FACE, and in a plot of innervation index vs arbor area the two distributions are non-overlapping.
source: SA-FACE arbors also have a lower mean innervation index than LA-FACE, and in a plot of innervation index vs arbor area the two distributions are non-overlapping (Figure 8C, right panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 8C.

claim: HD-FALE and LD-FALE are not clearly distinguished by the number of follicles innervated, but show a clear separation in a plot of innervation index vs arbor area.
source: The two classes of arbors with lanceolate endings, HD-FALE and LD-FALE are not clearly distinguished by the number of follicles innervated (Figure 8C, left panels), but show a clear separation in a plot of innervation index vs arbor area (Figure 8C, right panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 8C.

claim: Cutaneous sensory arbors are precisely stratified and each arbor type has a characteristic depth.
source: Figures 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1 show that cutaneous sensory arbors are precisely stratified and that each arbor type has a characteristic depth.
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The outer arbors of the BE and LA-FE classes reside close to the skin surface, most likely within the epidermis, and their inner arbors reside approximately 70 μm from the skin surface.
source: The outer arbors of the BE and LA-FE classes reside close to the skin surface, most likely within the epidermis, and their inner arbors reside ∼70 μm from the skin surface.
evidence: The claim is based on measurements from the experimental data.

claim: TE arbors are located approximately 20 μm from the skin surface.
source: TE arbors are located ∼20 μm from the skin surface.
evidence: The claim is based on measurements from the experimental data.

claim: Follicle associated circular and lanceolate endings reside approximately 50 μm from the skin surface for non-guard hair follicles and approximately 40 μm from the skin surface for guard hair follicles.
source: Follicle associated circular and lanceolate endings reside ∼50 μm from the skin surface for non-guard hair follicles and ∼40 μm from the skin surface for guard hair follicles.
evidence: The claim is based on measurements from the experimental data.

claim: This work is the first systematic description of sensory afferent morphologies in vertebrate skin.
source: The work reported here is the first systematic description of sensory afferent morphologies in vertebrate skin.
evidence: The claim is stated as a summary of the contribution.

claim: The 10 arbor types characterized from mouse back skin likely provide a still incomplete picture of cutaneous arbor diversity.
source: The 10 arbor types characterized from mouse back skin cover a wide range of morphologies but likely provide a still incomplete picture of cutaneous arbor diversity for at least two reasons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the limitations of the study.

claim: The AP reporter and CreER driver used here are expressed in many but not all DRG neurons.
source: First, the AP reporter and CreER driver used here are expressed in many but not all DRG neurons (Badea et al., 2012); and, second, body surfaces such as the lips, cornea, nipples, genitalia, and glabrous skin were not included in the survey.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Badea et al., 2012.

claim: Body surfaces such as the lips, cornea, nipples, genitalia, and glabrous skin were not included in the survey.
source: First, the AP reporter and CreER driver used here are expressed in many but not all DRG neurons (Badea et al., 2012); and, second, body surfaces such as the lips, cornea, nipples, genitalia, and glabrous skin were not included in the survey.
evidence: The claim describes the scope of the study.

claim: Each sensory arbor exhibits a high degree of uniformity in its terminal structures.
source: One important result from this survey is that each sensory arbor exhibits a high degree of uniformity in its terminal structures.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experimental data.

claim: Arbors with lanceolate endings never produce circular endings, bushy endings, or thick endings.
source: Thus, arbors with lanceolate endings never produce circular endings, bushy endings, or thick endings; arbors with circular endings never produce lanceolate endings, bushy endings, or thick endings; and so on.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experimental data.

claim: Arbors with circular endings never produce lanceolate endings, bushy endings, or thick endings.
source: Thus, arbors with lanceolate endings never produce circular endings, bushy endings, or thick endings; arbors with circular endings never produce lanceolate endings, bushy endings, or thick endings; and so on.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experimental data.

claim: The only possible exception to the pattern of terminal structure uniformity is the presence of occasional free nerve endings within arbors that have follicle-associated circular endings (LA-FACE arbors).
source: The only possible exception to this pattern is the presence of occasional free nerve endings within arbors that have follicle-associated circular endings (LA-FACE arbors; Figure 6B,C).
evidence: The claim is based on observations from Figure 6B,C.

claim: The morphologic uniformity of terminal structures within each arbor type argues for a corresponding uniformity in the sensory transduction apparatus and in the range and types of favored stimuli.
source: The morphologic uniformity of terminal structures—presumably the sites of transduction of the sensory stimulus—within each arbor type argues for a corresponding uniformity in the sensory transduction apparatus and, consequently, in the range and types of favored stimuli.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the morphological observations.

claim: Cutaneous sensory afferents represent a set of labeled lines, collectively delivering to the dorsal spinal cord at least 10 parallel representations of external stimuli that impinge on hairy skin.
source: Thus, these data support the view that cutaneous sensory afferents represent a set of labeled lines, collectively delivering to the dorsal spinal cord at least 10 parallel representations of external stimuli that impinge on hairy skin.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the morphological observations.

claim: MCA arbors likely correspond to the A-beta slowly adapting type I/low threshold mechanoreceptors (SA I/SA LTMRs) that contact Merkel cell clusters/touch domes.
source: MCA arbors likely correspond to the A-beta slowly adapting type I/low threshold mechanoreceptors (SA I/SA LTMRs) that contact Merkel cell clusters/touch domes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from known physiological and anatomical correlations.

claim: I-FALE arbors that surround guard hair follicles likely correspond to A-beta rapidly adapting (RA) LTMRs.
source: I-FALE arbors that surround guard hair follicles likely correspond to A-beta rapidly adapting (RA) LTMRs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from known physiological and anatomical correlations.

claim: HD-FALE arbors likely correspond to A-beta RA LTMRs that innervate awl/auchenne hair follicles.
source: HD-FALE arbors likely correspond to A-beta RA LTMRs that innervate awl/auchenne hair follicles.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from known physiological and anatomical correlations.

claim: I-FACE, LA-FACE, and SA-FACE arbors likely correspond to the peptidergic and/or nonpeptidergic circumferential free nerve endings described by Fundin et al. (1997).
source: I-FACE, LA-FACE, and SA-FACE arbors likely correspond to the peptidergic and/or nonpeptidergic circumferential free nerve endings described by Fundin et al. (1997); the physiologic correlates of this class are, at present, unknown.
evidence: The claim is based on inference and citation to Fundin et al. (1997).

claim: The physiologic correlates of I-FACE, LA-FACE, and SA-FACE arbors are, at present, unknown.
source: I-FACE, LA-FACE, and SA-FACE arbors likely correspond to the peptidergic and/or nonpeptidergic circumferential free nerve endings described by Fundin et al. (1997); the physiologic correlates of this class are, at present, unknown.
evidence: The claim is stated as a limitation of current knowledge.

claim: TE arbors could correspond to the thickened endings of myelinated fibers referred to by Rice and colleagues as 'fuzzy endings' or 'club endings', which are suggested to represent mechanoreceptors.
source: TE arbors could correspond to the thickened endings of myelinated fibers referred to by Rice and colleagues as 'fuzzy endings' or 'club endings', which are suggested to represent mechanoreceptors (Fundin et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and citation to Fundin et al. (1997).

claim: BE and LA-FE arbors come close to and may partially penetrate the epidermis.
source: The two types of arbors with free endings—BE and LA-FE arbors—come close to and may partially penetrate the epidermis (Figure 8D), a characteristic that is shared with a variety of peptidergic and nonpeptidergic fibers with free endings, including C-type nociceptors and thermoreceptors.
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 8D.

claim: BE arbors bear a particularly close resemblance to the arbors of MrgprB4-expressing neurons.
source: BE arbors bear a particularly close resemblance to the arbors of MrgprB4-expressing neurons, one of a large number of Mrgpr-expressing neurons that together mediate the sense of itch (Liu et al., 2007, 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and citations to Liu et al., 2007, 2009.

claim: MrgprB4-expressing neurons are one of a large number of Mrgpr-expressing neurons that together mediate the sense of itch.
source: BE arbors bear a particularly close resemblance to the arbors of MrgprB4-expressing neurons, one of a large number of Mrgpr-expressing neurons that together mediate the sense of itch (Liu et al., 2007, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2007, 2009.

claim: For I-FALE and I-FACE arbors that target single guard hair follicles, sensory information is gathered at single follicle resolution with a sampling pattern based on the regular mosaic of guard hairs.
source: For those I-FALE and I-FACE arbors that target single guard hair follicles, the clear prediction is that sensory information is gathered at single follicle resolution with a sampling pattern based on the regular mosaic of guard hairs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the morphological observations.

claim: LA-FE neurons are predicted to have receptive fields of 3–5 mm diameter with dense and relatively homogeneous coverage by sensory endings.
source: At the opposite extreme, LA-FE neurons are predicted to have receptive fields of 3–5 mm diameter with dense and relatively homogeneous coverage by sensory endings.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the morphological observations.

claim: BE neurons are predicted to have receptive fields of 0.5–1 mm diameter with an even higher density of sensory endings.
source: BE neurons are predicted to have receptive fields of 0.5–1 mm diameter with an even higher density of sensory endings.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the morphological observations.

claim: Spatial resolution is predicted to be relatively low for HD-FALE arbors, each of which contacts most follicles within its approximately 0.5 to approximately 1 mm diameter territory.
source: Spatial resolution is also predicted to be relatively low for HD-FALE arbors, each of which contacts most follicles within its ∼0.5 to ∼1 mm diameter territory; these afferents presumably sense hair deflections.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the morphological observations.

claim: HD-FALE afferents presumably sense hair deflections.
source: Spatial resolution is also predicted to be relatively low for HD-FALE arbors, each of which contacts most follicles within its ∼0.5 to ∼1 mm diameter territory; these afferents presumably sense hair deflections.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the morphological observations.

claim: Many HD-FALE endings cover only part of the circumference of their associated follicle, suggesting that two or three HD-FALE arbors might co-innervate a single follicle.
source: Many HD-FALE endings cover only part of the circumference of their associated follicle, suggesting that two or three HD-FALE arbors might co-innervate a single follicle and, therefore, that deflection of a single hair might elicit synchronous responses in several HD-FALE arbors.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the morphological observations.

claim: Deflection of a single hair might elicit synchronous responses in several HD-FALE arbors.
source: Many HD-FALE endings cover only part of the circumference of their associated follicle, suggesting that two or three HD-FALE arbors might co-innervate a single follicle and, therefore, that deflection of a single hair might elicit synchronous responses in several HD-FALE arbors.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the morphological observations.

claim: For any given HD-FALE and LD-FALE arbor, the C-shaped territories of different lanceolate clusters generally reside on the same side of their associated follicles.
source: For any given HD-FALE and LD-FALE arbor, the C-shaped territories of different lanceolate clusters generally reside on the same side of their associated follicles (Figures 4A–C and 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 4A–C and 8E.

claim: The asymmetric localization of lanceolate endings suggests a corresponding asymmetry in mechanosensory responses.
source: This asymmetric localization suggests a corresponding asymmetry in mechanosensory responses.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the morphological observations.

claim: If hair deflection toward a lanceolate ending elicits a response opposite to that of hair deflection away from the lanceolate ending, then the asymmetric locations of lanceolate endings would provide information about the direction of hair movement.
source: By analogy with the responses of auditory and vestibular sensory cells, if hair deflection toward a lanceolate ending ('compression') elicits a response opposite to that of hair deflection away from the lanceolate ending ('extension'), then the asymmetric locations of lanceolate endings would necessarily provide information about the direction of hair movement.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation by analogy with other sensory systems.

claim: A coherent wave of mechanical stimulation would presumably elicit a response of the same polarity from multiple similarly oriented C-shaped endings.
source: A coherent wave of mechanical stimulation—the sort delivered by a large object moving over the body surface—would presumably elicit a response of the same polarity from multiple similarly oriented C-shaped endings.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from the morphological observations.

claim: If direction-selective responses exist in lanceolate endings, they would provide the somatosensory system with an information stream analogous to that provided to the visual system by direction selective retinal ganglion cells.
source: If such a direction-selective response exists it would provide the somatosensory system with an information stream analogous to that provided to the visual system by direction selective retinal ganglion cells (Vaney et al., 2012), except that the proposed directionality of the cutaneous sensor would derive from structural asymmetry at the nerve ending/hair follicle complex rather than by spatiotemporal comparisons among neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and citation to Vaney et al., 2012.

claim: The proposed directionality of the cutaneous sensor would derive from structural asymmetry at the nerve ending/hair follicle complex rather than by spatiotemporal comparisons among neurons.
source: If such a direction-selective response exists it would provide the somatosensory system with an information stream analogous to that provided to the visual system by direction selective retinal ganglion cells (Vaney et al., 2012), except that the proposed directionality of the cutaneous sensor would derive from structural asymmetry at the nerve ending/hair follicle complex rather than by spatiotemporal comparisons among neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from the morphological observations.

claim: The pattern of spatially asymmetric C-shaped lanceolate clusters is especially striking among LD-FALE arbors because the innervated follicles are spaced at large intervals (approximately 0.5 mm).
source: The pattern of spatially asymmetric C-shaped lanceolate clusters is especially striking among LD-FALE arbors because the innervated follicles are spaced at large intervals (∼0.5 mm), a distance that would appear incompatible with any direct communication between endings.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experimental data.

claim: LD-FALE neurons would represent excellent candidates for the C-fiber neurons that subserve affective touch stimuli of the sort elicited by a mother licking her pups.
source: If, as seems probable, the LD-FALE neurons sense coherent hair deflections with low spatial resolution, then these neurons would represent excellent candidates for the C-fiber neurons that subserve affective touch stimuli of the sort elicited by a mother licking her pups (Andrew, 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and citation to Andrew, 2010.

claim: Similar C-fiber responses to low force, slowly moving stimuli—referred to as 'pleasant touch'—have been recorded from human hairy skin by microneurography.
source: Similar C-fiber responses to low force, slowly moving stimuli—referred to as 'pleasant touch'—have also been recorded from human hairy skin by microneurography (Johansson et al., 1988; Löken et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Johansson et al., 1988 and Löken et al., 2009.

claim: LA-FACE arbors exhibit a pattern of dense follicle coverage, with approximately 60% of follicles contacted in a territory of approximately 2 mm diameter.
source: A pattern of dense follicle coverage is seen in LA-FACE arbors, with ∼60% of follicles contacted in a territory of ∼2 mm diameter.
evidence: The claim is based on measurements from the experimental data.

claim: There are clear differences among follicles in the number of AP+ circumferential fibers, with some follicles encircled by only one or two fibers whereas others exhibit a thick band of AP staining at least 10 times the intensity of an individual fiber.
source: Although AP histochemistry cannot resolve individual fibers within a tightly packed circumferential bundle, there are clear differences among follicles in the number of AP+ circumferential fibers, since some follicles appear to be encircled by only one or two fibers whereas others exhibit a thick band of AP staining that is at least 10 times the intensity of an individual fiber.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experimental data.

claim: If each follicle receives roughly the same total number of circumferential fibers, then many follicles receive fibers from two or more LA-FACE arbors.
source: If we suppose that each follicle receives roughly the same total number of circumferential fibers, then these data suggest that many follicles receive fibers from two or more LA-FACE arbors, as described above for HD-FALE arbors.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the morphological observations.

claim: The coverage factor for HD-FALE arbors would be between one and two.
source: The average HD-FALE arbor contacts >80% of follicles within its territory and its sensory endings occupy on average >50% of the circumference of each follicle. If we assume that each follicle's circumference is fully and uniformly occupied by lanceloate endings—an assumption supported by high resolution light and electron microscopic imaging (Casserly et al., 1994; Takahashi-Iwanaga, 2000; Li et al., 2011)—then the coverage factor for HD-FALE arbors would be between one and two.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the morphological observations and citations to Casserly et al., 1994, Takahashi-Iwanaga, 2000, and Li et al., 2011.

claim: Each follicle's circumference is fully and uniformly occupied by lanceolate endings.
source: If we assume that each follicle's circumference is fully and uniformly occupied by lanceloate endings—an assumption supported by high resolution light and electron microscopic imaging (Casserly et al., 1994; Takahashi-Iwanaga, 2000; Li et al., 2011)—then the coverage factor for HD-FALE arbors would be between one and two.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Casserly et al., 1994, Takahashi-Iwanaga, 2000, and Li et al., 2011.

claim: The coverage factor for HD-FALE arbors might be somewhat higher since lanceolate endings from different arbors interdigitate extensively, with the result that an individual follicle may accommodate more than two half-circles of lanceolate endings.
source: This number might be somewhat higher since it appears from the work of Li et al. (2011) that lanceolate endings from different arbors interdigitate extensively, with the result that an individual follicle may well accommodate more than two half-circles of lanceolate endings.
evidence: The claim is based on inference and citation to Li et al. (2011).

claim: The coverage factor for LA-FACE arbors is estimated to be 2–4.
source: A somewhat less precise estimate of the coverage factor can be made for LA-FACE arbors since the extent of coverage of an individual follicle by AP-stained circumferential endings is more difficult to estimate than the extent of coverage by clusters of lanceolate endings. On the assumption that every follicle receives a level of circumferential fiber coverage that roughly corresponds to the highest levels observed in our samples, and with each LA-FACE arbor encircling ∼60% of follicles within its territory, we estimate a coverage factor of 2–4.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the morphological observations.

claim: LD-FALE arbors could potentially have coverage factors of >30.
source: Following the same logic, LD-FALE arbors could potentially have coverage factors of >30 since they innervate hair follicles that are spaced at intervals of ∼0.5 mm (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the morphological observations.

claim: The estimate of coverage factor >30 for LD-FALE arbors represents an upper limit, since LD-FALE arbors are presumably competing for follicle targets with HD-FALE arbors.
source: However, this estimate represents an upper limit, since LD-FALE arbors are presumably competing for follicle targets with HD-FALE arbors.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the morphological observations.

claim: The mechanisms that determine laminar specificity, target specificity, and arbor size and branching density among cutaneous afferents are unknown.
source: In particular, the mechanisms that determine laminar specificity, target specificity, and arbor size and branching density among cutaneous afferents are unknown.
evidence: The claim is stated as a limitation of current knowledge.

claim: Questions about developmental mechanisms may be especially tractable in systems in which arbors are confined to one or several parallel planes, as in the inner plexiform layer of the vertebrate retina and the Drosophila larval body wall.
source: While these and related questions have been addressed in a wide variety of neurobiological systems, they may be especially tractable in systems in which arbors are confined to one or several parallel planes, as in the inner plexiform layer of the vertebrate retina and the Drosophila larval body wall (Masland, 2001, 2011; Jan and Jan, 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and citations to Masland, 2001, 2011 and Jan and Jan, 2010.

claim: Competition among arbors of the same type for a limited pool of targets or target territories could determine the size of individual arbor territories.
source: For sensory arbors that contact multiple follicles, competition among arbors of the same type for a limited pool of targets or target territories—such as the finite circumference of each follicle, around which the lanceolate endings are packed—could determine the size of individual arbor territories.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about developmental mechanisms.

claim: Competition has been described among lanceolate endings that innervate the same guard hair follicle.
source: Competition of this sort has been described among lanceolate endings that innervate the same guard hair follicle (Casserly et al., 1994), and it is analogous to the competition observed among motor axons at the developing neuromuscular junction (Turney and Lichtman, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Casserly et al., 1994 and Turney and Lichtman, 2012.

claim: Competition among lanceolate endings is analogous to the competition observed among motor axons at the developing neuromuscular junction.
source: Competition of this sort has been described among lanceolate endings that innervate the same guard hair follicle (Casserly et al., 1994), and it is analogous to the competition observed among motor axons at the developing neuromuscular junction (Turney and Lichtman, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Turney and Lichtman, 2012.

claim: A competition model predicts that the average arbor territory will correlate inversely with, and be controlled by, the number of DRG neurons of the given class per unit area of skin.
source: This model predicts that the average arbor territory will correlate inversely with, and be controlled by, the number of DRG neurons of the given class per unit area of skin.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the competition model.

claim: Axon length and number of branch points vary over a 1,000-fold range across different arbor types.
source: Finally, axon length and number of branch points, which vary over a 1,000-fold range across different arbor types, could be controlled not only by local extrinsic signals but also by regulating, at the level of gene transcription, the abundances and ratios of various cytoskeletal proteins (Gallo, 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on measurements from the experimental data.

claim: Axon length and number of branch points could be controlled by regulating, at the level of gene transcription, the abundances and ratios of various cytoskeletal proteins.
source: Finally, axon length and number of branch points, which vary over a 1,000-fold range across different arbor types, could be controlled not only by local extrinsic signals but also by regulating, at the level of gene transcription, the abundances and ratios of various cytoskeletal proteins (Gallo, 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and citation to Gallo, 2011.

claim: Hair follicles and their associated structures—Merkel cell clusters (touch domes), arrector pili muscles, and sebaceous glands—are all polarized with respect to the body axes.
source: Hair follicles and their associated structures—Merkel cell clusters (touch domes), arrector pili muscles, and sebaceous glands—are all polarized with respect to the body axes.
evidence: The claim is based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: The anterior-to-posterior angle of the hair follicle is under the control of the planar cell polarity pathway.
source: This is macroscopically apparent in the anterior-to-posterior angle of the hair follicle itself, an organizational feature that is under the control of the planar cell polarity pathway (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2010.

claim: Each hair follicle could transmit polarity information to its associated lanceolate cluster.
source: It seems reasonable to suppose that each hair follicle could transmit polarity information to its associated lanceolate cluster, and recent experiments with mice lacking planar cell polarity signaling in the skin support this conjecture (Chang and Nathans, unpublished observations).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and unpublished observations.

claim: Recent experiments with mice lacking planar cell polarity signaling in the skin support the conjecture that hair follicles transmit polarity information to lanceolate clusters.
source: It seems reasonable to suppose that each hair follicle could transmit polarity information to its associated lanceolate cluster, and recent experiments with mice lacking planar cell polarity signaling in the skin support this conjecture (Chang and Nathans, unpublished observations).
evidence: The claim is based on unpublished observations.

claim: The primary sensory neurons of the cutaneous sensory system are abundant, large, and anatomically segregated in the DRG.
source: First, the primary sensory neurons are abundant, large, and anatomically segregated (in the DRG) where they can be studied or dissected either during development or in adulthood.
evidence: The claim is based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: The sensory arbors of the cutaneous sensory system are embedded within a large two-dimensional tissue (the skin) that is readily accessible to controlled stimulation or surgical and pharmacologic manipulations.
source: Second, the sensory arbors are embedded within a large two-dimensional tissue (the skin) that by virtue of its surface location is readily accessible to controlled stimulation or surgical and pharmacologic manipulations.
evidence: The claim is based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: The cutaneous sensory system is the only sensory system in which single unit recordings can be made from primary sensory neurons in an awake human to correlate physiology with psychophysics.
source: And third, it is the only sensory system in which single unit recordings can be made from primary sensory neurons in an awake human to correlate physiology with psychophysics (e.g., Vallbo and Johansson, 1984; Vallbo et al., 1984; Löken et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vallbo and Johansson, 1984, Vallbo et al., 1984, and Löken et al., 2009.

claim: Previous histochemical and immunolocalization studies on skin have generally been conducted with vertically sectioned tissue.
source: Unlike previous histochemical and immunolocalization studies on skin that have generally been conducted with vertically sectioned tissue (e.g. Fundin et al., 1997; Zylka et al., 2005), we have worked exclusively with intact skin.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fundin et al., 1997 and Zylka et al., 2005.

claim: Murine skin is sufficiently thin that intradermal structures can be imaged in their entirety, obviating the need for physical sectioning.
source: First, murine skin is sufficiently thin that intradermal structures can be imaged in their entirety, thus obviating the need for physical sectioning.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the properties of murine skin.

claim: The two-dimensional nature of the skin sample and the resiliency of fixed skin simplifies tissue handling, imaging, and cataloguing of structures by their location in the X–Y plane.
source: Second, the two-dimensional nature of the sample and the resiliency of fixed skin simplifies tissue handling, imaging, and cataloguing of structures by their location in the X–Y plane.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental experience.

claim: The relative ease with which large areas of skin can be surveyed in flat mounts facilitates the assembly of large datasets and the identification of relatively rare arbor types.
source: And third, the relative ease with which large areas of skin can be surveyed in flat mounts facilitates the assembly of large datasets and the identification of relatively rare arbor types.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental experience.

claim: The present morphologic survey of cutaneous afferents represents one facet of a larger program aimed at systematic structural analyses of nervous tissue.
source: The present morphologic survey of cutaneous afferents represents one facet of a larger program aimed at systematic structural analyses of nervous tissue.
evidence: The claim is stated as context for the work.

claim: Compared to other neuronal reconstruction programs, the analysis of cutaneous sensory arbors has an important simplifying feature: interactions between different arbors are minimal.
source: Compared to other neuronal reconstruction programs, the analysis of cutaneous sensory arbors has an important simplifying feature: interactions between different arbors are minimal (perhaps limited to co-innervation of the same target follicle) so that a full appreciation of the neuroanatomy can largely be obtained from reconstructions of individual arbors and their epithelial targets.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the morphological observations.

claim: A full appreciation of the neuroanatomy of cutaneous sensory arbors can largely be obtained from reconstructions of individual arbors and their epithelial targets.
source: Compared to other neuronal reconstruction programs, the analysis of cutaneous sensory arbors has an important simplifying feature: interactions between different arbors are minimal (perhaps limited to co-innervation of the same target follicle) so that a full appreciation of the neuroanatomy can largely be obtained from reconstructions of individual arbors and their epithelial targets.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the morphological observations.

claim: In most regions of the nervous system, connectivity between large numbers of pre- and postsynaptic partners is critical to understanding neuronal function.
source: By contrast, in most regions of the nervous system, connectivity between large numbers of pre- and postsynaptic partners is critical to understanding neuronal function.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge of neuroscience.

claim: In the not-too-distant future, it should be possible to obtain a comprehensive anatomic description of cutaneous afferents in mammalian skin.
source: This simplifying feature, together with the technical advantages of two-dimensional imaging and reconstruction in the skin, suggests that, in the not-too-distant future, it should be possible to obtain a comprehensive anatomic description of cutaneous afferents in mammalian skin.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about future research.

source: Brn3aCKOAP/CKOAP mice were crossed to NFL-IRES-CreER/NFL-IRES-CreER mice.

source: Mice were sacrificed at P21, and the back was shaved and treated with hair remover.

source: Back skins were dissected intact and pinned dermal side up to a flat Sylguard surface using insect pins.

claim: Skins were heated to 70°C for 90 min to inactivate endogenous phosphatase activity.
source: Subdermal connective tissue was removed with fine forceps, and the skins were fixed overnight in 4% paraformaldehyde in phosphate buffered saline (PBS), and then heated to 70°C for 90 min to inactivate endogenous phosphatase activity.

source: AP histochemistry and clearing in benzyl benzoate:benzyl alcohol (2:1) (BBBA) were performed as described in Badea et al. (2003), (2012).

source: For long-term storage, skins were equilibrated in ethanol at −20°C.

source: To survey arbor areas, a montage of each skin was first assembled from images obtained with a dissecting microscope.

source: For high resolution analyses, including axon tracing, BBBA-cleared skins were flattened between two glass gel-electrophoresis plates and isolated arbors were imaged at 10× magnification on a Zeiss apotome system.

source: Grey-scale Z-stacks were captured in bright field mode with a 5 μm separation between adjacent layers.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods.

claim: Following dehydration in ethanol and clearing in BBBA, adult skin showed essentially no shrinkage in the X- and Y-dimensions and was reduced to approximately 92% of the original thickness in the Z-dimension.
source: Following dehydration in ethanol, with the skin still pinned to the Sylguard surface, and clearing in BBBA, adult skin showed essentially no shrinkage in the X- and Y-dimensions and was reduced to ∼92% of the original thickness in the Z-dimension.
